parts.intro: You will hear a telephone conversation between a receptionist at a health centre and a man who wants to register as a new patient.

turns.text: Good morning, Hollybank Health Centre. How can I help you?
Hi. I've just moved to the area and I'd like to register as a patient with you, please.
Of course. I can take your details now over the phone, and then we'll book you in for a new patient check. Can I start with your name?
Yes, it's Daniel Ferrant.
Could you spell the surname for me?
Sure. It's F-E-R-R-A-N-T.
Two Rs?
That's right. Two Rs in the middle, and just one N near the end.
Thank you. And your date of birth?
The fourteenth of March, nineteen ninety-one.
Lovely. And what's your new address?
It's Flat 3, 28 Quarry Lane. Oh, sorry, no, it's Quarry Road. Quarry Lane is where my sister lives. I always mix them up.
No problem. Quarry Road. That's inside our area, good, we cover all the streets up to the river. Can I ask what you do for a living? We ask because some jobs carry particular health risks.
I'm an electrician. I used to work in a factory, but these days I'm mostly on building sites.
Electrician, thanks. Now, do you have any allergies we should know about?
Yes, I'm allergic to penicillin. I found out when I was a child. I'm fine with other antibiotics, as far as I know.
Penicillin. I've marked that clearly on your record. Are you taking any regular medication?
Just an inhaler. I've had asthma since I was a teenager, but it's quite mild. I only use it a couple of times a week, a bit more in winter.

Asthma, okay. The nurse will want to review that at your check. So, let's book that now. The nurse runs new patient checks on Tuesday and Thursday mornings, but Tuesday this week is fully booked, I'm afraid.
Thursday's better for me anyway. I start work late on Thursdays.
Right. I've got a quarter past nine or a quarter to ten.
Quarter past nine might be a rush with the school traffic. Could I take the later one?
Yes, so that's Thursday at 9.45 with Nurse Lindqvist.
Great. Do I need to bring anything? I've already sent you a copy of my tenancy agreement to prove my address.

That's fine for the registration. For the check itself, please bring a list of any medicines you take, with the name and strength of your inhaler. You don't need your passport. And wear something with loose sleeves, because she'll take your blood pressure.
Okay. And when I need more inhaler, how do I get a repeat prescription? At my old surgery I had to phone up.

We stopped taking requests by phone last year, because the lines were always too busy. You can still drop a paper form in the box at reception, but most people use our online app now, and that's the quickest way, because it goes straight to the doctor. I'd recommend that.
I'll download it today. One last thing: what should I do if I'm ill at night or at the weekend?

When we're closed, please don't go to the hospital unless it's a real emergency. Phone the evening line instead. The number's on the back of the leaflet I'll post to you. A nurse there will tell you what to do, and they can book you an appointment with us for the next day.
Perfect. Thanks very much for your help.
You're welcome, Mr Ferrant. See you on Thursday.

parts.intro: You will hear a shift manager giving an induction talk to new staff at a warehouse.

turns.text: Morning, everyone, and welcome to Westgate Distribution. I'm Karen, and I'm one of the three shift managers here. Over the next twenty minutes I'll give you the basics you need before you go out onto the floor this afternoon.

First, a bit about the site. We used to handle mostly food for supermarkets, but these days it's mainly household goods: cleaning products, kitchenware, that sort of thing. There's talk of building a second warehouse next door, but that won't happen for a couple of years. What matters for you is that we run twenty-four hours a day, Monday to Saturday. On Sundays the building is closed so the maintenance team can service the machines.

Now, shifts. Normally there are three: early, six till two; late, two till ten; and nights. But for your first two weeks you'll all be on the early shift, so that there's always a trainer and a supervisor around to answer questions. I know some of you were hoping to start on nights straight away, and you'll get your chance, but not in your first fortnight. After that you'll go onto the normal rota, which changes every month.

You'll see the rota on the staff app. A lot of people think they can swap shifts on the app, but you can't; it only shows you the rota. If you need to swap, you can arrange it with a colleague, but the swap doesn't count until a manager has approved it, and we need at least two days' notice. Turning up for someone else's shift without approval means neither of you gets paid properly, so please don't do it.

Right, safety. When I ask new staff what causes most accidents here, they always say forklifts. And of course we take forklifts very seriously. But actually, most of the injuries we had last year happened because people tripped over loose packaging: plastic wrap, straps, empty boxes left on the floor. So put rubbish in the bins as you go. Lifting injuries used to be our biggest problem, but since we brought in the lifting training they've dropped right down.

If you see a spill, don't try to clean it up straight away. You may not know what it is, and some of the cleaning products we store can burn your skin. The first thing to do is put one of the yellow warning cones beside it, so nobody walks through it. Then tell a supervisor, and they'll decide how it should be cleaned.

Finally, let me run through the different areas, because each one has its own rule. At the loading bay, lorries are reversing all day. The alarms are loud, and there are ear plugs in the box by the door if you want them, but they're your choice. The rule you must follow there is that you don't use your mobile phone at all, not even to check the time, because you need your eyes on the vehicles.
The cold store is kept at minus eighteen degrees. There are jackets hanging by the door, and you have to put one on before you go in, even if you're only popping in for a minute. No exceptions.

You'll spend most of your time in the picking aisles. The forklifts use the same aisles, so you must keep to the green walkways painted on the floor. Step outside them and you're in the forklift lane.

The staff canteen is the only place you can eat or drink, apart from water bottles. Because we handle food for one of our clients, there's a sink at the entrance, and everyone has to wash their hands as they go in.

And the battery charging room, where the forklifts are charged: only staff with a forklift licence are allowed in, because the batteries give off gas and need careful handling. If your trolley needs charging, ask a driver.

The offices upstairs are where visitors usually go, and any visitor must have someone from the company with them, but that won't affect you much. Okay, let's take a short break, and then we'll go and look round.

parts.intro: You will hear two adult learners, Marta and Joel, talking to a course adviser at a community college about evening courses.

turns.text: Hi, come on in. You're Marta and Joel? Great. So you're both interested in our evening program this fall. Marta, maybe you could start. What are you hoping to get out of a course?

Well, everyone assumes I want to change careers, but actually I'm happy with what I do. I run a small cake stall at the weekend market, and it's growing, and I need to be able to handle the business side myself. At the moment my brother does my accounts, and I'd like to stop relying on him.
That makes sense. And Joel?

For me it's partly about meeting people. I moved here in the spring and I don't know many people yet. The fees are okay, I think. My employer said they might pay part of it. My real worry is the timing. I start work at six in the morning, so anything that finishes after nine is going to be difficult for me.

Okay, most of our classes run from seven to nine, but a few go until nine thirty, so we'll keep an eye on that. And about fees, there's a twenty percent reduction if you sign up for two courses at the same time. We did have an early payment discount too, but I'm afraid that ended last week.
Two courses, that's interesting. When do we need to decide by?
Enrollment was supposed to close this Friday, but because so many people came in late, it's been extended to next Monday. So you have a few days.
Is it possible to try a class first? I don't want to pay and then find it's not right for me.
Yes, most courses offer a free trial class in the first week.
Then I'd really like to go to one before I enroll. Last year I paid for a yoga class and gave up after two weeks.

Good idea. Okay, let me tell you about the courses you both marked on your forms. Joel, you were interested in Digital Photography. It's a very popular course, but be aware that it isn't held here on the main campus. It's taught at the Arts Center on River Street, because they have the darkroom and the lighting studio.
That's across town. Hmm, okay.

Marta, Bookkeeping for Small Businesses sounds perfect for you. It used to include a two-week work placement in a local firm, but that was dropped last year. What it does do is prepare you for the national bookkeeping exam, so at the end you get a certificate that employers and banks recognize.
That would be useful when I apply for a loan.

Then Spanish for Beginners. Joel, you mentioned that. The classroom group finishes at nine thirty, which might be too late for you. But there's also an online version of the same course, with live lessons from home.
That might work, actually.

Furniture Restoration. Marta, you ticked that too? It's a lovely course, very practical. The tutor provides the tools, but you'll need to buy your own wood, paint, and varnish, so materials cost extra, usually around sixty dollars over the term.
That's fine. I've got an old chair I'd love to fix up.

And finally Creative Writing. Most of our courses run for twelve weeks, but this one is only six weeks long, so it's a good taster if you're not sure about committing for a whole term. People sometimes think it's full because Pottery, which runs on the same night, filled up in a day, but there are still places in Creative Writing.
Okay. I think I'll go for the online Spanish, and maybe Photography as well, if I can get across town in time.
And I'll come to the trial class for Bookkeeping on Tuesday and decide after that.

parts.intro: You will hear part of a lecture about the history of public libraries.

turns.text: Good afternoon. Today I want to look at how the public library, something most of us take for granted, actually came into being, and how its role has kept changing.

Collections of books are, of course, very ancient, but for most of history they belonged to monasteries, universities or wealthy individuals, and ordinary people had no right to use them. In the eighteenth century a new model appeared in many towns: the subscription library. Groups of middle-class readers pooled their money to buy books they could not afford alone. Each member paid a yearly fee, and in return could borrow from the shared collection. These libraries tended to stock serious works such as history, travel and science.

Alongside them grew up what were called circulating libraries, which were run as businesses, often by booksellers. They charged a small sum per book, and their great attraction was lending novels, which were expensive to buy and which the subscription libraries often refused to stock. Critics at the time complained that circulating libraries encouraged young people to waste their time, but they were enormously popular.

Neither of these, though, was a public library in the modern sense, because you had to pay. The real turning point came in the middle of the nineteenth century, when laws were passed in several countries allowing towns to collect a small tax from local households and spend it on a free library. It's worth stressing that these laws allowed towns to do this; they didn't force them, and many towns voted against it for decades.

Why the opposition? Some of it was simply about money. But there were other fears too. Later in the century, as people began to understand germs, some critics worried that books passed from hand to hand could spread disease. In a few places, books returned from homes where someone was sick were even burned.

The great expansion came around the turn of the twentieth century. Many towns could not afford a proper building from local taxes alone, and much of the money for construction came from wealthy donors, who often paid for the building on condition that the town would pay to run it. That's why so many older libraries look rather grand, with columns and steps at the front.

Inside, early public libraries worked very differently from today. Most used what was called closed access. Readers were not allowed near the books at all. Instead, they looked through a printed catalogue, wrote down the number of the book they wanted, and a member of staff fetched it. Some libraries even had a large board showing which books were in and which were out.

This gradually gave way to open access, where readers could browse the shelves themselves. Librarians at first were alarmed, expecting theft, but losses turned out to be small, and borrowing rose sharply. Open access, I'd argue, changed the library from a store of books into a place for discovery.

Another change in the early twentieth century was the arrival of separate rooms for children. Before that, many libraries had simply refused to admit anyone under fourteen. Children's rooms, with low shelves and story hours, helped to create the next generation of adult readers.

Libraries also tried to reach people far from towns. The earliest mobile services were actually horse-drawn carts carrying boxes of books from village to village. Motor vans replaced them later, and in some regions today boats and even bicycles do the same job.

So what about now? Libraries have had to argue for their place in a digital world. Many offer free internet access and help with online forms, which matters a great deal to people without a computer at home. And some have returned to their sharing roots in a surprising way: as well as books, they now lend unusual items such as tools, from drills to sewing machines, so that people don't have to buy something they'll use only once. In the second half of the lecture, we'll look at one such library in detail.

passages.title: Three local notices
passages.text:
A  CORRAN VALLEY BUSES: NEW PASS OFFERS

Whether you travel every day or only now and then, one of our passes could save you money. All passes can be bought from the driver, at the Central Bus Station ticket office, or through the CVB Go app.

Weekly Pass: £18
Unlimited travel for seven days from the first day of use. Valid on all our routes except the Airport Express, which has its own fares.

Monthly Pass: £62
Unlimited travel for a calendar month. If you no longer need your Monthly Pass, you can return it to the ticket office before the 10th of the month and we will refund half the price. After this date the full price is charged.

Student Pass: £45 per month
Available to anyone in full-time education aged 16 or over. Each time you board, you must show the driver a valid student card together with your pass. Without the card, you will be asked to pay the full single fare.

Family Day Pass: £14
Travel for up to two adults and three children under 16, any day of the week, including weekends and public holidays. All members of the group must travel together.

Please note: passes are personal and cannot be shared, except the Family Day Pass as described above. Lost passes can be replaced at the ticket office for a £5 charge, as long as you bring proof of purchase.

B  EASTFIELD COMMUNITY POOL: AUTUMN TIMETABLE

The main pool reopens on Monday 2 September after its summer repairs, and the new changing rooms are now fully open.

Public swimming
Monday to Thursday: 7.00 am to 9.00 pm
Friday: 7.00 am to 10.00 pm (late swim with music from 8.00 pm)
Saturday and Sunday: 8.00 am to 6.00 pm
The pool is closed on all public holidays.

Lane swimming
Three lanes are kept for lane swimming every weekday from 7.00 to 9.00 am and from 12.00 to 1.30 pm. Lanes are marked slow, medium and fast. Please choose the lane that suits your speed and always swim in a clockwise direction.

Children's lessons
Lessons for ages 5 to 11 run on Mondays, Tuesdays and Thursdays from 4.30 to 6.00 pm. Places are limited, so book at reception at least a week ahead. Children under 8 who are not in a lesson must be accompanied in the water by an adult at all times.

Pool rules
All swimmers with hair longer than shoulder length must wear a swimming cap. Caps are on sale at reception for £2. Please shower before entering the pool. Lockers in the changing rooms need a £1 coin, which you get back when you open the locker again. Valuables are left at your own risk.

Entry prices: adults £4.50, children £2.50.

C  BROOK STREET SECOND-HAND FURNITURE MARKET

Every Saturday, 9 am to 3 pm, Brook Street Hall

Looking for a sofa, a table for a new flat, or a set of shelves? The Brook Street market brings together around forty sellers, from families clearing out their homes to small businesses that repair and restore old furniture. Prices are usually far below those in shops, and many sellers are happy to discuss them.

Buying
Payment is by cash or card at most tables, and a cash machine is available in the entrance hall. Large items that you have bought can be left in the storage room until 4 pm, when the hall closes. Please collect them by then, as anything left after this time will be returned to the seller. Our volunteer team can deliver items within six miles of the hall for an extra charge of £15 per trip; ask at the information desk.

Safety
All electrical items, such as lamps and heaters, are tested by a qualified volunteer electrician before they go on sale, and carry a green 'tested' sticker. Other furniture is sold as seen, so check items carefully before you pay.

Selling
Tables for sellers cost £12 for the day and must be booked by the Wednesday before. Sellers should arrive by 8.15 am to set up. We cannot accept mattresses, or any upholstered furniture without a fire safety label.

Free parking is available behind the hall.

passages.title: Two staff guides
passages.text:
REQUESTING ANNUAL LEAVE: A GUIDE FOR STAFF

All full-time employees at Harrowgate Freight are entitled to 25 days of paid annual leave each year, in addition to public holidays. Part-time staff receive the same entitlement in proportion to the hours they work. The leave year runs from 1 January to 31 December.

How to make a request
All requests must be made through the staff portal, which you can reach from any work computer or from your own phone. Paper forms are no longer accepted. Your request goes automatically to your line manager, who will normally reply within three working days. Do not book travel or make any payments that cannot be refunded until your leave has been approved.

How much notice to give
For leave of one to five days, give at least two weeks' notice. For anything longer than five days, the minimum is four weeks. Requests made at shorter notice may still be approved, but only if your team has enough cover.

Busy periods
Some weeks are especially popular, particularly in July and August and around the end of the year. To keep things fair, if more people ask for the same week than the team can release, a ballot is held, and the names drawn are given priority. Staff who are unsuccessful in a ballot will be given first choice the following year.

Carrying leave over
We encourage everyone to take their full entitlement within the year. However, up to five days of unused leave may be carried over into the following year, provided they are used by the end of March. Any further unused days will be lost.

Other types of leave
In an emergency, such as a sudden family illness, you should phone your line manager before the start of your shift; a text message or email is not enough. Time off for medical or dental appointments is paid, but where possible appointments should be booked at the start or end of a shift to reduce disruption. Requests for unpaid leave, for example for an extended trip abroad, must be approved by Human Resources (HR) as well as by your manager.

WORKPLACE FIRST-AID KITS: WHAT YOU NEED TO KNOW

Every site has at least one first-aid kit, and every member of staff should know where the nearest one is kept. Kits are green boxes marked with a white cross, and their locations are shown on the notice board beside each entrance.

Who looks after the kits?
Each site has an appointed first-aider, whose name is displayed next to each kit. Although anyone may use a kit in an emergency, it is the first-aider's job to check the contents and keep them up to date. Other staff should not move kits or take items from them for any purpose other than first aid.

Checking and refilling
Kits are checked once a month, and the date of each check is written on the card inside the lid. Whenever you use anything from a kit, write what you took in the logbook kept with it, so that the first-aider knows what needs replacing. Items such as sterile dressings have an expiry date and must be thrown away once it has passed.

What a kit contains
A standard kit includes plasters in various sizes, sterile eye pads, bandages, disposable gloves, safety pins and cleansing wipes. You will not find tablets or medicines of any kind, including common painkillers. This is because some people react badly to particular medicines, and first-aiders are not trained to decide which drugs are safe for someone else to take.

Larger kits and extra equipment
Where staff work with machinery or sharp tools, such as in the workshop and on the loading dock, larger kits are provided, along with eye-wash stations. The size of a kit depends on the level of risk rather than simply on the number of people working in an area.

Travel kits
Drivers who spend their working day on the road are each issued with a small travel kit to keep in their vehicle. If you are a driver and your kit is used or damaged, report it to the transport office, which will replace it.

passages.title: Before the Fridge: How People Kept Food
passages.text:
Before the Fridge: How People Kept Food

A  In many countries the home refrigerator became common only in the second half of the twentieth century, and in large parts of the world it is still far from universal. Yet for thousands of years before that, people managed to store food through the winter, carry it on long journeys and save the surplus from a good harvest. They did so using a handful of techniques, most of which are still in use today, often without our noticing. What all of them have in common is that they make life difficult for the bacteria and moulds that cause food to spoil.

B  Drying is probably the oldest of all these methods. Microbes need water to grow, and if enough moisture is removed from meat, fish, fruit or grain, decay slows almost to a stop. In hot, dry regions the sun and wind did the work naturally. In coastal communities further north, fish were split and hung on wooden racks in the cold, windy air, where they could become so hard that they lasted for years. Dried fruit, meanwhile, had the added advantage of becoming sweeter as its sugars were concentrated, making it a valuable food for travellers.

C  Salting works in a similar way. When food is packed in salt, water is drawn out of it, and the salty environment that remains is one in which few harmful organisms can survive. Because salt made it possible to keep meat and fish for months, it became one of the most valuable goods in the ancient and medieval world. Roads were built to transport it, and governments in many places taxed it heavily. Salted fish and meat fed sailors and soldiers far from home, although such food was hardly a pleasure to eat: it often had to be soaked in fresh water for many hours before it could be cooked.

D  Smoking may well have begun by accident. Food hung near a fire to keep it away from animals would have dried out faster, and people would have noticed that it also lasted longer. We now know that wood smoke contains chemical compounds that slow the growth of bacteria and stop fats from turning bad. For a long time, then, smoking was mainly a practical measure, and the distinctive flavour it gives to fish, meat and cheese only later became valued in its own right. Today, smoked foods are often eaten for their taste alone, and many are smoked so lightly that they must still be kept cold.

E  Fermentation and pickling take a different approach. Rather than trying to remove all microbes, they encourage useful ones. When vegetables are kept in salty water, or milk is left in the right conditions, friendly bacteria multiply and produce acid, and this acid prevents harmful organisms from taking hold. Pickling in vinegar achieves a similar result more directly. Fermented foods such as yoghurt and pickled cabbage are found in cuisines all over the world, and some ship captains carried barrels of fermented vegetables on long voyages in the belief that they kept their crews healthy.

F  Cold storage itself is not a modern idea. Long before electricity, wealthy households built ice houses: partly underground buildings into which blocks of ice, cut from frozen lakes in winter, were packed with straw or sawdust as insulation. Well-built ice houses could keep ice solid well into the summer. In the nineteenth century the ice trade became a major industry, and ice was shipped across oceans to much warmer countries. In hot, dry climates a much cheaper method was used: a clay pot placed inside a larger one, with wet sand between them. As water evaporates from the outer pot, it draws heat away from the inner one, which can keep vegetables fresh for days longer than they would last in the open air.

G  The last major technique arrived in the early nineteenth century, when a government at war offered a prize to anyone who could find a better way of feeding its armies. The winning method was to seal food in glass jars and then heat them for a long time. Remarkably, the process worked decades before anyone could explain why: it was only later in the century that scientists showed that heating killed the microbes inside, and that the seal prevented new ones from entering. Glass was soon replaced by metal cans, which were lighter and did not break. The first cans, however, were so thick that they had to be opened with a hammer and chisel; a proper can opener did not appear until almost fifty years later.

H  For much of the twentieth century these older methods were seen as old-fashioned, replaced by the convenience of the freezer. Recently, however, they have attracted fresh interest. They use little or no energy, which matters both to people who care about the environment and to the many households whose electricity supply is unreliable. They also offer a way of using up a large harvest instead of throwing it away, and so help to reduce food waste. And for many people, the flavours they create are reason enough to keep them alive.

tasks.prompt:
You should spend about 20 minutes on this task.

The heater in the flat you rent has stopped working, and it is now very cold.

Write a letter to your landlord. In your letter
- describe the problem with the heater
- explain how this problem is affecting you
- say what you would like your landlord to do

Write at least 150 words.

Begin your letter as follows:

Dear Mr Halloway,

You should spend about 40 minutes on this task.

Write about the following topic:

Many people now work in a country where a different language is spoken. Some people believe that employers should pay for these workers to take language classes, while others think that workers should pay for their own training.

What is your opinion?

Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience.

Write at least 250 words.

questions: Do you work or are you a student?
What do you like most about your work or studies?
Is there anything you would like to change about your work or studies?
Do you think you will do the same kind of work or study in the future? Why or why not?
Do you enjoy cooking? Why or why not?
Who usually cooks in your home?
What was the first dish you learned to cook?
Would you like to take cooking lessons one day?

parts.cue_card:
Describe a journey you made that did not go as planned.
You should say:
- where you were going and why
- who you were with
- what went wrong during the journey
and explain how you felt about the journey afterwards.

questions: Why do you think some journeys go wrong even when people plan them carefully?
How has public transport in towns and cities changed in recent years?
Should governments spend more money on public transport or on building new roads? Why?
Some people say that cheap air travel is bad for the environment. What is your view?
How do you think the way people travel to work will change in the next twenty years?
Is travelling to other countries still as important for young people as it was in the past?
